To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
GH suppression did not prevent exercise-induced improvement in cardiorespiration and mitochondrial oxidative function in young female rats.
exercise training improves cardiorespiratory and mitochondrial function in rats despite the suppression of GH and IGF-1 secretion.
exercise training improves maximal oxygen consumption and endurance time in rats, even when normal GH function is suppressed.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of growth hormone (GH) in the adaptation to aerobic exercise.
the effects of growth hormone suppression on exercise and growth responses in young rats.
the effect of GH suppression on exercise-induced changes in cardiorespirator function in young rats.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
GH does not appear to be required for training-induced improvements in maximal oxygen uptake and mitochondrial function in growing female rats.
exercise-induced improvements in cardiorespiratoy function and mitochondrial function occur in the absence of GH.
the GH axis is not necessary for training-induced improvements in exercise performance or in mitochondrial function in the young growing rat.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
GH does not appear to play an important role in the exercise-induced improvement of maximal aerobic capacity and mitochondrial function.
exercise training improves cardiorespiratory performance in young female rats despite suppression of pituitary GH secretion.
the GH/IGF-I axis does not appear to play a major role in the adaptation to treadmill exercise training in young female rat pups.
The main takeaway from our work is that
exercise training improves cardiorespiratory fitness in young rats, even when GH is suppressed by anti-GH-releasing hormone antisera.
